entry.title: How AppFlowy Works: Inside the Rust and Flutter Notion Alternative

link.title: How AppFlowy Works: Inside the Rust and Flutter Notion Alternative

entry.content:
Your Notion workspace lives on Notion’s servers. Offline mode is limited, sync is a black box, and if their API or pricing changes, your carefully linked databases go with it. AppFlowy — the AGPL-licensed open-source Notion alternative — takes the opposite trade: the same kind of workspace, but the backend is a Rust library compiled into your app, documents are CRDT files on your own disk, and the server is strictly optional. The whole thing is one repository you can clone and read.

This post walks the AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy source at its main branch with two generated architecture diagrams. The first is a 12-node overview that follows the stack from Flutter widgets down to SQLite. The second is a 32-node detail map of the pieces that actually matter: the FFI bridge, the event dispatcher, the eight domain plugins, the yrs CRDT layer, and the optional AppFlowy Cloud sync. Every node in the SVGs links to the real file on GitHub, and every symbol quoted below was verified against the tree at commit time.

By the end you’ll know how a keystroke in the editor becomes a protobuf event, crosses dart:ffi into Rust, gets routed to one of eight plugins, lands in either Diesel-managed SQLite or a yrs CRDT document, and — only if you opted in — syncs over a WebSocket. If you’ve followed our earlier source tours of Rust codebases or TypeScript web apps, this one is interesting precisely because it refuses to be a web app.

Overview: the Flutter UI talks protobuf over FFI to the Rust core, which routes events through plugins into SQLite and the yrs collab layer, with cloud sync as a detachable group on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The root container is one struct. AppFlowyCore, L61 holds managers for users, folder, documents, databases, search, AI and storage, plus the event_dispatcher and a server_provider. Its init at AppFlowyCore::new, L86 assembles every dependency before the UI renders a single widget.
  • The Dart side boots Rust first. InitRustSDKTask, L13 serialises paths, device id and cloud config into a JSON AppFlowyConfiguration, and FlowySDK.init, L37 registers two Dart ports before calling init_sdk natively.
  • There is exactly one C entry point for startup. init_sdk, L114 parses that JSON, spawns a dedicated OS thread running a Tokio runtime inside a LocalSet, and constructs the whole AppFlowyCore there.
  • Everything after startup is request/response over FFI. Dart’s Dispatch.asyncRequest, L53 writes a protobuf request to bytes, allocates an FFI buffer, and hands over a completion port; Rust’s async_event, L175 picks it up and posts the response bytes back to the same port.
  • One dispatcher, no routing framework. AFPluginDispatcher, L63 keeps a map of plugins and, via async_send, L79, finds whichever plugin registered the event id on the request.
  • Eight plugins cover the whole product. make_plugins, L12 returns user, folder, database, document, date, search, AI and file-storage plugins — and each one takes only Weak references to the managers, so the dispatcher never owns domain state.
  • Events are protobuf enums, not strings. DocumentEvent, L59 declares 21 numbered events from CreateDocument = 0 to GetDocumentText = 20, each with typed protobuf input and output declared via derive macros.
  • Metadata lives in SQLite under Diesel. init, L32 opens flowy-database.db (named at DB_NAME, L30) and runs embedded Diesel migrations on every launch.
  • Content lives in CRDT collabs, not SQLite. AppFlowyCollabBuilder, L76 builds one yrs-backed Collab per document, grid or board, flushed to disk by write_collab_to_disk, L363.

Detail: the full round trip — Dart launch tasks and blocs, the generated FFI bindings, the Rust dispatch loop, the plugin registries, the managers behind them, and the collab/cloud groups where edits become CRDT updates.

The Rust core: one dispatcher, eight plugins

frontend/rust-lib is a Cargo workspace of ~25 crates: lib-dispatch is the event bus, flowy-core is the composition root, and the rest are domain crates (flowy-folder, flowy-document, flowy-database2, flowy-user, flowy-ai, flowy-search, flowy-storage) plus plumbing (flowy-error, flowy-sqlite, dart-ffi). The plugin model is refreshingly small: AFPlugin, L64 is a name, a state (the manager as Weak), and a list of handlers bound with an .event() builder at .event, L107. Registration reads like a table of contents: the folder plugin wires ~45 handlers from FolderEvent, L66 (view creation, moving nested views, trash, favorites), the database plugin from DatabaseEvent, L11 (fields, rows, cells, filters, sorts), the document plugin from DocumentEvent above.

Two details make this design hold up. First, errors are uniform: every handler returns FlowyResult<T>, where FlowyError, L17 wraps a numeric ErrorCode, L10 that survives the FFI hop as protobuf. Second, handlers never reach each other directly — the document plugin asks the database plugin’s manager through resolved dependencies in flowy-core/src/deps_resolve/, keeping the event graph acyclic. This is the same “thin framework, fat domain crates” pattern we liked in our Rust tour at /rust/, just with a Flutter front door.

The Dart side: protobuf bytes over dart:ffi

AppFlowy does not use method channels for its event traffic. The generated ffi.dart looks up async_event directly in libdart_ffi, and dispatch.dart does the wire format by hand: request.writeToBuffer() (protobuf), a calloc.allocate buffer, and ffi.async_event(port.nativePort, input, bytes.length) at dispatch.dart, L130. On the Rust side the bytes become an AFPluginRequest, the Runner loop spawns it as a local task, and the response goes back through post_to_flutter, L258, which posts FFI-encoded bytes onto the allo_isolate port Dart is awaiting.

That mechanism also runs backwards, continuously. FlowySDK.init registers a stream port at set_stream_port, L38, and Rust pushes notifications — document changes, sync state, user events — through a registered NotificationSender (register_notification_sender, L22). The Flutter layer is then classic flutter_bloc: DocumentBloc, L47 owns one open document, throttles selection sync at 250 ms, and funnels editor transactions into the same dispatch round trip. Every Dart call site is generated per module — dispatch.dart literally parts in dart_event/flowy-*/dart_event.dart files that mirror the Rust event maps, which is why adding an event means touching both sides and regenerating.

Where your data lands: SQLite for metadata, CRDT for content

AppFlowy splits persistence deliberately. Relational, queryable state — user profiles, workspace/view metadata, KV preferences — goes to SQLite through Diesel 2.1 (diesel with sqlite and r2d2 pool features at Cargo.toml, L75). Migrations are compiled into the binary (MIGRATIONS, L29) and applied in init before any handler runs, so a user upgrading the app always lands on the current schema. The per-user connection comes straight from the user session — get_sqlite_db, L370.

Document content never touches those tables. Each document, grid, board or calendar is a yrs CRDT whose updates are encoded and flushed by CollabPersistenceImpl (CollabPersistenceImpl, L417): write_collab_to_disk encodes the doc, then flush_doc writes the state vector and doc state inside one transaction (flush_doc, L384). DocumentManager keeps open documents in a DashMap<Uuid, Arc<RwLock<Document>>> at DocumentManager, L54, with open_document at open_document, L327. Undo/redo is a CRDT feature: collab.enable_undo_redo() is called when a document collab is built (enable_undo_redo, L169), which is why undo survives restarts. If you want the general pattern — when to keep data in SQLite versus beside it — we cover it in the SQLite post at /sqlite/.

Sync: yrs CRDT updates over an optional WebSocket

The local-first claim is enforced in code, not marketing. A workspace is either local or cloud — DocumentBloc checks WorkspaceTypePB.LocalW at isLocalMode, L102, and the Dart auth layer picks BackendAuthService(AuthTypePB.Local) versus AppFlowyCloudAuthService in one switch at currentCloudType, L107. With local auth, no network client is even constructed.

When you do enable sync, the pieces are conventional but cleanly separated. AppFlowyCloudServer::new at AppFlowyCloudServer, L62 builds a REST client (base URL, WebSocket URL, Auth0-style gotrue_url at AFCloudClient::new, L76) and the WSClient::new, L91 WebSocket client; spawn_ws_conn at spawn_ws_conn, L97 re-establishes the socket as tokens refresh. Open documents get one WebSocketChannel per object id via collab_ws_channel, L245. The CRDT engine itself is yrs, L98 — the Rust port of Yjs — pinned at 0.21.0, and finalize() attaches cloud sync plugins to a collab only when sync_enable is set (finalize plugins, L341). Because edits merge as CRDT updates rather than OT on a central server, offline edits replay cleanly when the socket returns.

From a TypeScript web app to a Flutter-first repo

One structural fact worth knowing before you dig in: earlier AppFlowy versions carried an in-tree TypeScript web client, but today’s main branch contains no package.json anywhere — the web frontend is no longer part of this repository, and the entire shipped frontend is the Flutter app plus the Rust workspace. That makes the repo unusual among Notion alternatives: instead of “web app first, Electron shell later”, every desktop and mobile target compiles the same Dart UI against the same native Rust library (README lists macOS, Windows and Linux downloads plus App Store and Play Store listings). The cost is visible in the numbers: git ls-tree -r HEAD on main counts ~2,700 files under frontend/appflowy_flutter and ~950 under frontend/rust-lib, with generated protobuf Dart under packages/appflowy_backend/lib/protobuf acting as the contract between them. If you are porting a web-first product, the TypeScript archives on this blog show the pattern AppFlowy moved away from — and the diagrams above show what a native-first split looks like instead.

Honest Limits

  • sync_event is a stub. The synchronous FFI entry point logs unimplemented sync_event and returns empty bytes at sync_event, L230 — every real interaction takes the async path, so there is no synchronous escape hatch for tools embedding the core.
  • Conflict handling admits gaps. The document bloc’s own comment says the logic “is not fully implemented yet” and forces state reloads via a sync timer (conflict comment, L98). CRDTs merge text reliably, but UI-level conflict UX is still defended with timers.
  • Undo/redo is not uniform across object types. It is enabled for document collabs at creation (enable_undo_redo above), but the folder builder path (create_folder, L200) does not enable it, so workspace-tree edits behave differently from document edits.
  • The AGPL core and the cloud are different codebases. The README pins this repo to AGPL-3.0 (license badge, L16); the server that powers AppFlowy Cloud sync lives elsewhere, so self-hosting the full stack means deploying a second project.
  • Everything above reflects main on 2026-11-17 — commit-verified line numbers, not documentation. AppFlowy moves fast; treat exact line anchors as a snapshot.
entry.summary: How AppFlowy works inside: the Rust event dispatcher, Dart FFI, Diesel SQLite storage, yrs CRDT sync and plugin system of the open-source Notion alternative.

entry.title: How Joplin Works: Inside the Open-Source Note App Architecture

link.title: How Joplin Works: Inside the Open-Source Note App Architecture

entry.content:
If your notes live in a proprietary cloud app, two things are true at once: you pay a monthly fee for the privilege of reading your own words, and getting them out means converting away from a private container format the vendor controls. Cloud note apps lock your notes in proprietary formats and charge monthly — Joplin keeps every note in open Markdown on SQLite and syncs to wherever you want: a local folder, a WebDAV or Nextcloud server, OneDrive, Dropbox, or the project’s own hosted cloud. It is free, open source under AGPL-3.0-or-later, and written entirely in TypeScript, which means every architectural decision is sitting in the repo waiting to be read.

This post is a guided tour of the laurent22/joplin source tree (default branch dev). The two diagrams below were generated from the actual repository structure: the overview shows how three frontends — desktop, terminal CLI, and a self-hostable server — all lean on one shared core library, and the detail diagram zooms into the SQLite storage layer, the sync engine with its FileApi adapters, the markdown-it rendering rules, and the plugin sandbox. Every node links to the real source file on GitHub, so you can jump straight from picture to code.

By the end you will know exactly how a note travels: keystroke in a React editor, row in a SQLite table, serialized item in a three-phase sync loop, rendered HTML on screen — and how third-party plugins hook into all of it without ever getting direct access to your database.

Joplin at a glance — three frontends extend one BaseApplication, all data flows through BaseItem models onto SQLite, and the Synchronizer pushes changes to interchangeable sync targets through a common FileApi.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • One BaseApplication, three frontends. The shared bootstrap lives at BaseApplication, L104 and the desktop app extends it at Application, L85 — window management, auto-update checks and Redux wiring all hang off that single start() at L818.
  • Notes are rows, not files. The Note, L72 model stores the raw Markdown body as a column value; Note.save, L966 is the single write path every frontend uses.
  • Everything syncable funnels through BaseItem. BaseItem, L63 is the parent of notes, folders, resources and tags; its serializeForSync, L527 flattens any item into the text format the sync layer uploads.
  • The sync engine is a three-step loop. Synchronizer, L87 — the comment above start, L404 documents the phases verbatim: UPLOAD, DELETE_REMOTE, DELTA, driven by the syncSteps array at L420.
  • Concurrent clients coordinate with locks. Before touching the remote, the engine calls acquireLock at L632 and auto-refreshes the lease at L634 — two laptops syncing to the same folder cannot corrupt each other.
  • Sync targets are pluggable adapters. BaseSyncTarget, L13 defines the contract; concrete targets include SyncTargetJoplinCloud, L16, SyncTargetOneDrive, L11, SyncTargetWebDAV, L17 and SyncTargetFilesystem, L8.
  • Markdown rendering is markdown-it plus app-aware rules. MdToHtml, L217 keeps a rule table at L42 — fence, KaTeX, mermaid, checkboxes — and registers each one into markdown-it in the merge loop at L599.
  • Plugins run sandboxed against a promise-based API. Plugins call register, L32 with an onStart handler; on desktop their code executes in an isolated iframe behind PluginRunner, L92, never in the main process.

The detail view: the desktop and CLI applications share the Redux reducer and settings model, the database layer offers two SQLite drivers, SearchEngine maintains an FTS4 index beside the tables, and the plugin framework isolates plugin code in a sandbox while exposing the JoplinPlugins API.

One shared core, three frontends

Joplin’s most consequential decision is the shape of packages/lib. It contains the models, the database wrapper, the synchronizer, the settings system and the plugin services, and every frontend imports it as @joplin/lib/.... The desktop UI’s main screen imports the shared reducer directly (MainScreen.tsx, L12), which is why a sidebar click and a CLI command end up mutating the same state shape.

The React layer is a classic Electron split: packages/app-desktop/app.ts runs in the main process (the Application class at L85), while MainScreenComponent at L96 renders the resizable layout and is glued to Redux with connect(mapStateToProps) at L519. The terminal app reuses the same BaseApplication from app-cli/app/app.ts, L28, swapping React for a text GUI — new AppGui(...) at L442 builds a status bar whose prompt() at app-gui.ts, L145 accepts ex-command-style input. Joplin Server, the self-hosted backend in packages/server, is an Express app that ends its boot with app.listen(config().port) at app.ts, L396 and ships its own schema.sqlite. If you enjoy this kind of repo mapping for TypeScript projects, the method transfers almost unchanged to other codebases — see /typescript-source/.

Notes live in SQLite, not a proprietary blob

The storage layer is refreshingly boring, in the best sense. packages/lib/database.ts wraps a single SQLite file: the Database class at L14 creates and migrates tables from a CREATE TABLE _TABLE_NAME_(_FIELDS_TYPE_) template at L363. Two drivers plug in underneath: DatabaseDriverNode at L17 uses the Node sqlite API via shim.nodeSqlite() at L22, while the better-sqlite3 driver at L38 exists as an alternative — its own header comments explain the trade-off around SQLITE_DQS=0.

Each entity is a plain model: Note, L72, Folder, L45 with a notebook tree rebuilt by allAsTree at L902, and Resource, L58 for attachments — binaries stay on disk as files, with only metadata in the table. Search is handled by SearchEngine at services/search/SearchEngine.ts, L97, which mirrors notes into an notes_fts FTS4 table (see the count(*) query at L359 and the matchinfo comments at L378). Because the store is a real relational database with a published schema, you can query your notes with any SQLite client — the notes are yours at the file level, not behind an API. The design contrasts nicely with server-only stores; for the fundamentals of that storage engine, see /sqlite/.

The Synchronizer: upload, delete_remote, delta

Synchronization is where Joplin earns its “your notes, anywhere” claim. Synchronizer.start() at L404 executes three phases, named in the code itself at L401–403: upload items changed locally since the last sync, delete_remote items deleted locally, and delta — pull remote changes by listing the target and applying differences. The step list is configurable at L420, and partial syncs skip the delta phase.

Because several devices may point at the same storage, the engine takes a sync lock before doing anything: this.lockHandler().acquireLock(LockType.Sync, ...) at L632, then starts auto-refreshing the lease at L634 so a long sync is not evicted mid-flight; a stuck lock from a dead client expires via TTL. The lock machinery itself is LockHandler at services/synchronizer/LockHandler.ts, L146. Items cross the wire as the flat text produced by serializeForSync at L527, and any item that cannot sync (an oversized resource, for instance) is flagged in the sync_disabled bookkeeping written by updateSyncTimeQueries at L920.

What makes the design durable is that the engine only talks to a FileApi — the abstraction at file-api.ts, L165 with put/get/list operations — and each backend implements it. The packages/lib folder ships eleven SyncTarget*.ts classes: Joplin Cloud and Joplin Server (including a SAML variant), OneDrive, Dropbox, WebDAV, Nextcloud (a WebDAV preset), the local file system, plus memory and no-op targets used in tests. Optional end-to-end encryption wraps the payloads in EncryptionService at services/e2ee/EncryptionService.ts, L89 — encryptFile at L744 and encryptString at L730 — so even a WebDAV folder you don’t control only ever stores ciphertext.

How markdown becomes HTML — and where plugins run

Rendering is a markdown-it wrapper with opinions. MdToHtml at L217 implements the MarkupRenderer interface and exposes render() at L462. Its rules table at L42–58 maps rule names to modules in MdToHtml/rules/: fenced code handling, KaTeX math, mermaid diagrams, checkboxes, images, sanitization. Each rule module exports a markdown-it plugin — the fence rule’s plugin(markdownIt) at rules/fence.ts, L15, KaTeX’s plugin factory at rules/katex.ts, L349. At render time the merge loop at L599 combines built-in and extra rules, skips disabled ones via pluginEnabled, and calls markdownIt.use(plugin, options) at L610 — which is how per-syntax settings like toggling ==mark== become real. A comment block above that loop, at L572–597, is effectively design documentation: it spells out the three ways a markdown plugin can hook in depending on whether it needs app data or toggleable settings.

Plugins get the same courtesy at the application level. PluginService at services/plugins/PluginService.ts, L92 loads packaged plugins and, notably, extracts the manifest from an embedded /* joplin-manifest: comment at L292–307 so a plugin is one script plus its metadata. The API a plugin sees is a tree of Joplin* classes — joplin.plugins.register({...}) at JoplinPlugins.ts, L32 fires the plugin’s onStart and emits started when it resolves. On desktop, execution is not in-process: PluginRunner at app-desktop/services/plugins/PluginRunner.ts, L92 marshals every call through executeSandboxCall (imported at L3) into a sandboxed iframe, so a buggy plugin crashes its own context, not your editor.

From Evernote importer to 27-package monorepo

Joplin started life as a note app with an Evernote import path — packages/lib/import-enex.ts still carries that heritage — but the repo has grown into a yarn-workspaces monorepo: the root package.json declares "workspaces": ["packages/*"] and pins engines to Node >=22.19 and yarn 4.17.0 (the terminal and server packages run on plain Node; for background on that runtime, see /node/). Counting package.json files under packages/ in the current tree yields 27 packages: the four frontends (app-desktop, app-cli, app-mobile, app-clipper), the shared lib, the renderer, the server, a standalone editor, plus support tooling — turndown and two forked libraries for HTML-to-Markdown conversion, an onenote-converter, transcribe and whisper-voice-typing for voice notes, generate-plugin-doc and generator-joplin for the plugin ecosystem, and the tools package that automates builds and translations. The whole tree is licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later by the root LICENSE file. The default branch is dev; every file cited in this post was verified there at commit 68b1f92.

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers drift. All citations reference branch dev at commit 68b1f92; the repository moves fast, so treat links as a snapshot.
  • Coverage is honest about scope. The tour concentrated on packages/lib, packages/app-desktop, packages/app-cli, packages/renderer and packages/server; packages/app-mobile (React Native) shares the same core but was not examined line-by-line here.
  • “Everything is Markdown” has an asterisk. Note bodies default to MarkupLanguage.Markdown, but the renderer family at MarkupToHtml.ts, L26 also carries an HTML source mode, and attachments are binary files referenced from rows — the openness applies to the store and format, not a claim that no other data exists.
  • Search is FTS4, not semantic. The classic path indexes into SQLite FTS4; semantic/embedding search exists alongside it (services/ai/EmbeddingIndexer.ts), but the default search matches on the FTS index.
  • No peer-to-peer sync. The eleven built-in target classes are the complete list; there is no git or P2P transport — extensibility comes from implementing the FileApi contract against a new backend.
entry.summary: How Joplin works: Electron/React desktop app, SQLite note store, the Synchronizer with pluggable sync targets, terminal CLI, plugin API, markdown-it rendering.

entry.title: How Logseq Works: Inside the Outliner and Datascript Architecture

link.title: How Logseq Works: Inside the Outliner and Datascript Architecture

entry.content:
Roam Research popularized networked note-taking — daily journals, bidirectional links, blocks you can refactor anywhere — but your knowledge base lives on someone else’s cloud, behind a subscription, in a format you cannot grep. Logseq answers that pain with a different bargain: the same outliner model, but your graph is stored on your own disk, and the entire application that manages it is open source. The current database version goes further than “plain files on disk”: a graph is a single SQLite database you can back up with one file copy, while Markdown export remains a derived, human-readable projection you can generate on demand.

Two diagrams in this post map that bargain onto the actual source tree. The overview traces the life of a keystroke: editor handler → outliner op → DB worker → in-memory Datascript → SQLite file, and back to the screen as immutable snapshots. The detail diagram adds the boot sequence, the schema and DataScript layer, the persistence backends (OPFS in the browser, files on the desktop), the query engine, and the plugin/SDK surface.

Reading this tour you will learn how a Lisp dialect (ClojureScript, compiled to JavaScript by shadow-cljs) runs a serious desktop app; why every paragraph you type is really an EDN datom; how the team moved graph ownership out of the renderer into a dedicated worker thread; how Datalog — not SQL, not a REST API — powers advanced queries; and what changed when Logseq migrated from Markdown-folder graphs to the SQLite-backed DB version. Every symbol cited below was verified against the master branch of logseq/logseq.

Overview: a keystroke crosses three boundaries — renderer to op layer, op layer to db worker, worker to SQLite — and returns as a snapshot diff.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • App entry. frontend.core/start, L74 mounts the root React component through the rfx provider; the namespace self-describes as the entry for “the mobile, browser and electron frontend apps” (ns docstring, L2).
  • Boot orchestration. frontend.handler/start!, L142 starts IndexedDB, registers plugin hosting, installs Electron IPC listeners, then kicks off persist-db/<start-runtime!, L171 and graph restore — a genuine “system component” in a codebase that otherwise favors pure functions.
  • The UI–worker bridge. frontend.state/<invoke-db-worker, L66 is the single choke point every renderer thread call takes to reach the worker; it throws immediately if the worker atom is not yet initialized.
  • Editor intent. frontend.handler.editor/save-block!, L1668 sits at the top of the tallest file in the frontend; its job is to translate caret state and user edits into outliner operations, not to touch the database.
  • Semantic ops. frontend.modules.outliner.op/transact!, L166 executes ops accumulated in a dynamic var by builders like save-block!, L36 — so a multi-block edit is one atomic batch, not N writes.
  • Ordered delivery. frontend.db.transact/apply-outliner-ops, L175 ships the batch to the worker as a thread-api request, after enqueue-outliner-mutation!, L26 chained it onto a per-repo promise tail so concurrent edits can never interleave.
  • The worker. frontend.worker.db-worker/init, L30 initializes the graph core inside a browser worker and exposes a Comlink proxy, L43 — the same pattern a REST server uses to own the database while clients render.
  • The database. logseq.db.common.sqlite/get-storage-conn, L23 restores an in-memory Datascript connection whose datoms are persisted through a storage layer backed by SQLite — Datascript for queries, SQLite for durability.
  • Queries. frontend.db.query-dsl/query, L40 shows that even simple query strings execute in the worker, keeping parser cost off the UI thread.

Detail: the same flow with boot, schema, persistence backends, queries and the plugin SDK included — node labels name real namespaces you can open on GitHub.

Why Every Note Is a Datom

Logseq’s core data model is not “pages containing text” — it is a graph of entities whose state is a set of EDN datoms: entity, attribute, value, transaction tuples held in Datascript, an in-memory database that implements the Datalog logic language. The outliner layer validates blocks against an explicit map of the fields that make a block a block: :block/uuid, :block/order, :block/parent and :block/page (block-map, L57). Nesting an outline is literally writing :block/parent datoms; reordering is rewriting :block/order. The same file’s save-block, L672, insert-blocks, L1099 and delete-blocks, L1395 are the primitive verbs of the whole app — everything else, from templates to task lists, compiles down to them.

Because the model is a database, features that other apps bolt on with string matching become queries. “All properties of this page” is an avet-index datom scan: get-all-properties, L42 reads :block/tags datoms directly. Breadcrumbs are a parent walk: get-page-parents, L47. This is the block graph model that made outliner tools famous, expressed as data rather than as a document format — the same philosophy we examined in the Node source tour, where module structure is likewise the primary data, except here even your notes are queryable facts. The batch-txs state, L4 in the outliner dep is where collected ops wait to become one transaction.

The DB Worker Split: Why the Renderer No Longer Owns Your Graph

The most consequential recent decision in this codebase is architectural, not feature-wise: the graph database lives in a dedicated worker thread, and the renderer holds only immutable snapshots. The worker’s entrypoint (init, L30) initializes the database core and exposes it over Comlink; the renderer-side subscription layer calls itself “Immutable renderer snapshots loaded from the worker-owned graph database” (ns docstring, L2) and warms an LRU cache of twenty thousand slots (warm-cache-size, L11) through batched loads like <load-block, L55.

The write path mirrors the read path. The frontend transact namespace serializes each repository’s mutations by chaining promises (enqueue-outliner-mutation!, L26) before transact, L162 dispatches the request; when the worker returns, deltas are applied to the renderer under react-dom/flushSync (publish-worker-response!, L147) so the caret never visibly lags. This split is why heavy operations — full-graph queries, schema restore, undo grouping — stopped janking the editor: they are worker-side by construction. The project records these decisions as ADRs, and the worker also owns undo/redo semantics per those documents.

Startup follows the same ownership rule: restore-graph!, L11 opens the graph “from SQLite” (docstring, L12), fetches the schema through the persistence backend, resolves sync conflicts, and only then resets renderer subscriptions. The renderer never loads raw datoms itself — it asks the worker.

Queries: From Query Blocks to Datalog

Logseq ships two query tiers, and both compile down to the database the worker owns. The DSL tier is what you write in query blocks on a page: the renderer namespace is explicitly a thin wrapper, “Query execution belongs to the db worker” (ns docstring, L2); query, L40 dispatches thread-api/query-dsl-query, and the custom-query variant, L52 handles the advanced form.

The advanced tier is real Datalog. The guard require-datalog-query!, L46 rejects anything that is not a proper query vector starting with :find (the :find check, L50), and the namespace titles itself the handler for “custom queries a.k.a. advanced queries” (ns docstring, L2). That means the full expressiveness of Datalog — rule bodies, joins across :block/parent chains — is available inside a note. This is the quiet superpower of storing notes as datoms: a “query” is not a plugin feature, it is the native interface of the storage engine, and Logseq just picks the executing thread.

From Plain-Markdown Folders to SQLite Graphs

This section is the build-facts record of Logseq’s biggest migration. The classic released Logseq — still what most users run — treats a folder of Markdown and Org files as the source of truth: files are parsed by the mldoc parser (a separate Logseq project wrapped in ClojureScript, “taking and returning edn” only, logseq.graph-parser.mldoc, L2) and the AST is turned into transactions during import (graph-parser.extract docstring, L2). In that world, Datascript was rebuilt by re-parsing your files at startup, and sync meant file syncing.

The DB version on master inverts that: the source of truth is a SQLite file, addressed as get-db-full-path, L49 mapping a graph to its db.sqlite, and Datascript datoms persist through a storage table with (addr, content, addresses) rows created by create-kvs-table!, L10 for use with datascript.storage (docstring, L11). Fresh graphs are stamped out by schema helpers in logseq.db.sqlite.create-graph, L2 — built-in classes, properties and typed property values — and graph-kind checks lean on db-version-prefix, L308. The README marks the DB version beta while mobile and real-time collaboration mature (README, L71), and the dependency list wires the pieces together: the Datascript fork (deps.edn, L10), the outliner library (deps.edn, L45) and the db-sync library (deps.edn, L46).

Markdown survives, but demoted to a projection. ADR 0016 specifies an Electron-only mirror that writes derived Markdown under mirror/markdown/journals/ and mirror/markdown/pages/ (ADR 0016) — with the explicit rule that “the DB remains the source of truth” and mirror files feed back into nothing. If you want to understand how a durable local store can back an editor, the SQLite engine behind this design is itself worth a source tour.

Plugins and the Electron Shell

The extension surface is a second ClojureScript namespace reserved for third parties: logseq.api, L2 is documented as “Logseq API for plugins usage” and exports dozens of hooks — slash command registration (register_plugin_slash_command, L53), storage files, user settings, UI items. The host installs during boot via handler.plugin/setup!, L1341. DB-version-specific plugin calls live in logseq.api.db-based, L2 (“DB version related fns”), which routes page and property mutations through the same outliner core the editor uses — plugins get no side door into the database, and block APIs even namespace their properties (plugin.property prefix, L17) to keep plugin data distinguishable from user data. Compared with the compiler-checked, type-first approach we covered in the TypeScript source tour, this is a runtime-gated API: flexible for authors, stricter at the boundary.

On the desktop, the same ClojureScript bundle runs inside Electron. The renderer talks to the main process through electron.ipc/ipc, L28, which serializes payloads as transit strings before calling window.apis.doAction (doAction call, L33) — one typed channel instead of dozens of ad-hoc bridges. The main process owns filesystem primitives (native db.sqlite files, plugin directories, the Markdown mirror), while all content logic stays in the worker per the ADR.

Honest Limits

  • Master is the DB-version branch. The SQLite graph, worker split and mirror ADR describe current master; the classic file-version code paths largely live in release branches and history. Treat master as fast-moving — the README itself steers stability-seekers elsewhere.
  • DB version is beta. The README says data loss is possible and recommends backups; real-time collaboration is in alpha. The sync libraries exist in-tree (db-sync dep, L46) but the surrounding product surface is explicitly unfinished.
  • The Markdown mirror is one-way. Editing mirrored files does not update the graph, per ADR 0016; it is an export, not round-trip sync, and browser/mobile builds do not get it.
  • Datascript is still in memory. Durability comes from the SQLite storage layer, so very large graphs trade RAM for query speed; the kvs-table design (create-kvs-table!, L10) is the boundary where that trade is managed.
  • Docs drift. src/main/frontend/persist_db/README.md still describes the older in-memory mental model, so older tutorials can disagree with newer code about where the database lives.
entry.summary: How Logseq works inside: the ClojureScript outliner frontend, Datascript EDN datoms on SQLite, the DB worker split, Datalog queries and the plugin API.

entry.title: How NocoDB Works: Inside the Airtable Alternative Architecture

link.title: How NocoDB Works: Inside the Airtable Alternative Architecture

entry.content:
Your production data already lives in a Postgres or MySQL instance, carefully backed up, replicated, and monitored. Then a teammate wants “something like Airtable” for it, and the conventional answer is to export tables into a SaaS spreadsheet, run nightly sync scripts, and accept that the two copies drift apart the moment someone edits either side. Row caps, API rate limits, and per-seat pricing pile on top of the real problem: the spreadsheet never touches the database you actually run. NocoDB’s open-source bet is that this copy step is unnecessary — it boots a NestJS server, connects to your existing database as one more client, and serves a Vue spreadsheet UI whose every cell reads and writes that database in place.

This post is a source tour of how that works, verified line by line against the nocodb/nocodb repository on its develop branch. The overview diagram below traces the full request path: the Vue grid in packages/nc-gui, the NestJS controllers and services in packages/nocodb, the Knex-based SQL engine, and the two storage layers — the nc_ metadata tables and your own data. The detail diagram then zooms into each layer, from the server bootstrap down to individual view models.

If you have ever wondered what “Airtable alternative” means structurally — where the smart spreadsheet ends and the database begins, which tables NocoDB creates, and how a filter you click in the UI becomes a WHERE clause — the next two diagrams and five sections answer exactly that, with links into the source at every step.

Overview: a click in the Vue grid travels through the NestJS controller and service layers into BaseModelSqlv2, which builds Knex queries against your database, while all spreadsheet metadata stays in the separate nc_ tables.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The server entry point is Noco.init, L165, which calls NestFactory.create, L166 with AppModule and a disabled body parser — NestJS boots on top of the plain Express instance created in bootstrap, L17, so there is exactly one HTTP server and one process.
  • Every spreadsheet operation arrives as REST: DataTableController, L26 maps GET /api/v2/tables/:modelId/records, L30 and POST records, L75 — the same endpoints the frontend SDK calls.
  • Controllers are thin: DataTableService.dataList, L58 resolves the model and view, then hands off to DatasService, L49, which owns actual row execution.
  • The bridge between metadata and SQL is Model.getBaseModelSQL, L649: it reads the model’s column definitions and constructs new BaseModelSqlv2, L693 with the driver for that source.
  • BaseModelSqlv2, L326 is the row engine — list, insert (insert, L2455), update, delete, link resolution — built as knex query builders, never raw string SQL.
  • Queries flow through a customized Knex: conditionv2, L1625 is a QueryBuilder extension that compiles NocoDB’s nested filter tree objects into WHERE clauses, and the whole module is exported as XKnex, L1698.
  • Database connections are pooled per source by NcConnectionMgrv2, L27, which keeps an LRU of drivers, L35 and builds each one with XKnex(config), L189 on first use.
  • The spreadsheet layer itself lives in MetaService, L41 — a knex instance over config.meta.db (metaDbConfig, L63) that reads and writes the nc_*_v2 tables declared in the MetaTable enum, L1, including nc_bases_v2 (L2), nc_grid_view_v2 (L34), and nc_kanban_view_v2 (L36).

Detail view: the bootstrap chain, the controller→service→model funnel, the SQL engine internals, and the Vue composables — 33 nodes covering every layer cited in this post.

The request path: from a grid cell to a Postgres query

Consider the smallest unit of work: the user types into a cell and the grid saves it. In the frontend, the grid surface wires its data through useViewData, L228, a composable defined in useViewData.ts, L13 whose loadData function issues api.dbViewRow.list, L266 — a typed SDK call against /api/v2/tables/:modelId/records. The virtualized InfiniteTable.vue, L272 keeps calling loadData({ offset, limit }) as you scroll, so pagination is just offset queries against the real table.

On the server, that request lands in the controller, moves through the service, and reaches BaseModelSqlv2, which knows three things: the table’s real name and columns (from metadata), the active view’s filters and sorts (also from metadata), and a knex driver for the source. It composes those into one SQL statement and sends it through the source’s pool. Relation fields — the linked-records columns that make a spreadsheet “smart” — get special treatment: the engine attaches batched loaders guarded by a serial queue (PQueue, L445, default concurrency 1) so resolving hundreds of link cells cannot exhaust the pool.

The HTTP plumbing is worth a pause because it is unusual for a NestJS codebase. NocoDB disables Nest’s body parser and mounts the Nest app as middleware inside an explicitly created Express server — the same one that later serves the built GUI from public/. If you want to see how much behavior hides inside that adapter layer, I traced Express’s internals separately in the Express source walkthrough; here it means one listening socket, no duplicate middleware, and direct access to req.ip for proxy-aware auditing (configured around L225 in Noco.ts).

The meta layer: nc_ tables that never touch your data

NocoDB’s own storage is deliberately small and boring. All of it — workspaces, bases, sources, models, columns, views, hooks, tokens, ACLs — is rows in tables prefixed nc_, named centrally in the MetaTable enum, L1. The v0 migration nc_001_init.ts, L1081 creates nc_bases_v2 with a nc_bases_v2_pkey composite primary key; every later schema change ships as an additional numbered migration file applied by migrate.latest, L1204.

By default this metadata store is a single SQLite file — NcConfig initializes meta.db to SQLite, L16 with filename: 'noco.db' at L18 — which is why a fresh NocoDB deployment works with zero external setup. The SQLite file format is what makes that safe as a config store: single-writer access, plain SQL, trivially backed up. Operators who outgrow it set NC_DB to a Postgres or MySQL URL instead, and MetaService runs identically on top because everything goes through the same knex builder (metaDbConfig, L63).

Every metadata write is workspace/base-scoped by construction: metaInsert2, L350 stamps fk_workspace_id and base_id onto each row and rejects inserts outside valid root scopes, while reads go through metaGet2/metaList2, which append the same scoping WHERE clauses. Record ids are generated per table by genNanoid, L156 using a prefix map (p for bases, m for models, c for columns, vw for views, kv for kanban views) — a small touch that makes every id in the metadata store self-describing in logs and URLs.

Views are metadata, not tables

The most instructive design decision in NocoDB is that grid, kanban, gallery, form, calendar, and timeline views are not data structures of their own — they are metadata projections over the same underlying table. The ViewTypes mapping, L106 in View.ts dispatches each view type to its own nc_*_view_columns_v2 metadata table: grid columns to nc_grid_view_columns_v2, kanban to nc_kanban_view_columns_v2, and so on through nine view types. Creating a view inserts rows there (View.insert, L362), never a new data table.

Each type keeps its specifics in a dedicated model: GridView, L16 stores flags like showSystemFields, KanbanView, L25 stores the stacking column configuration. The frontend consumes this split naturally — the kanban board loads through KanbanOptimized.vue, L547 calling loadKanbanData from a store that groups rows server-side via dbViewRow.groupedDataList, L763, so the stack grouping happens as one GROUP BY query against your database rather than a client-side sort of everything.

This is also why switching between grid and kanban feels instant: the rows are identical, only the projection changes, and filters/sorts are just additional knex clauses injected through the conditionv2 extension before the query executes. When a new column is added, ViewsService syncs column metadata into every existing view so all projections stay consistent — spreadsheet semantics implemented as a handful of small SQL statements.

From Airtable copies to in-place SQL (build facts)

For builders evaluating or extending NocoDB, the load-bearing facts are these. The backend is Node.js with knex 3.1.0 pinned at L142 and dedicated drivers for mysql2, L152, pg, L179, and sqlite3, L197 — the three databases it can attach to as data sources. The web framework pair is @nestjs/core 10.x at L70 with express 4.x at L118, and the whole thing runs in one Node process, so understanding its concurrency model matters before you scale it; my notes on the Node.js event loop cover the ground rules it inherits.

So the transformation NocoDB performs is precise: your table becomes a Model row, your columns become Column rows, your constraints stay in your database untouched, and the smart-spreadsheet experience is recomputed on every request from nc_ metadata plus live queries. Nothing replicates your rows. If you delete a column in NocoDB’s UI, it runs DDL against your database; if you edit a cell, it is an UPDATE on your table — the same consequences as editing via psql, with the spreadsheet as the client.

Two practical consequences follow. First, backup strategy is unchanged — your data backups are still your database backups, plus one extra small artifact (the noco.db meta file or NC_DB instance) that you should snapshot separately, since it holds views, permissions, and hooks. Second, performance is your database’s performance: the grid is as fast as the queries knex emits against your indexes, and no intermediate store will mask a missing index on a column you filter by.

Honest Limits

  • NocoDB reads your schema through its source models but stores its understanding of columns in nc_columns_v2; schema changes made outside NocoDB are not magically reflected — the metadata and the real schema are two stores that the sync/model-diff services reconcile, and drift there is a real operational surface.
  • The serial query queue (concurrency 1 by default) protects pools but also caps parallelism for relation-heavy requests; it is tunable via NC_DB_QUERY_QUEUE_CONCURRENCY per the code at BaseModelSqlv2, L445, and raising it trades throughput against pool exhaustion.
  • Satellite metadata (audit, chat, docs, operation logs) can live on separate databases when environment variables are set, and mixing transactions across them fails loudly by design — the guard is at assertSatelliteNotInMetaTrx, L115.
  • BaseModelSqlv2 dialect handling (for example the per-database random ordering in shuffle, L2421) shows the engine must special-case MySQL, Postgres, SQLite, MSSQL, and Oracle; exotic engines beyond the three shipped drivers are not a drop-in.
  • The metadata id generator uses nanoid variants of fixed length (L33-L38 in meta.service.ts); ids are short by design, so nothing in the nc_ store is intended to be globally unique across independent deployments — merges of two metadata stores are not a supported operation.
entry.summary: How NocoDB turns any MySQL, Postgres, or SQLite database into an Airtable-style smart spreadsheet: NestJS backend, Knex queries, and nc_ meta tables.

entry.title: How Outline Works: Inside the Team Wiki Architecture

link.title: How Outline Works: Inside the Team Wiki Architecture

entry.content:
Ask three people where the API spec lives and you will get three different answers: a Slack thread nobody can find anymore, a Google Doc whose owner left the company, and a Notion page that needs a login half the team does not have. Outline attacks exactly that pain. It is an open-source team wiki that companies self-host, backed by their own PostgreSQL, so every doc, revision and permission lives in one searchable place instead of scattering across SaaS silos. And it is not a weekend toy: the monorepo ships a Node.js and Koa API server, a realtime collaboration server, and a rich editor built from one shared ProseMirror package.

Two diagrams in this post map that promise onto the real source tree. The overview follows a single edit from the React client through a Hocuspocus WebSocket connection into the persistence extension that snapshots the Yjs document back into Postgres, while REST endpoints and Bull queues fan out the consequences. The detail diagram opens the box further: the collaboration extension chain, the four Redis queues with their processors, the SSO auth plugins, and the tsvector indexes that make full-text search a database feature rather than an add-on.

By the end you will know why Outline stores the same document three different ways (ProseMirror JSONB, Yjs state BLOB, search vector), how one keystroke becomes an update, then a revision, then a backlink without ever leaving Postgres, and where the code draws the boundary between the API path and the realtime path. Every symbol cited below carries a line anchor and was verified against the main branch of outline/outline.

Overview: the React client edits through a shared ProseMirror core; realtime edits ride Hocuspocus into Postgres via the persistence extension, REST calls hit the Koa API, and Bull queues on Redis drive the background processors.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The client is React, but the editor is not “a div”. MultiplayerEditor, L87 constructs a CollaborationProvider, L52 — an HocuspocusProvider subclass — per document, bundling socket lifecycle, awareness state and Yjs sync into one object the editor consumes.
  • One editor core shared by client and server. The shared/editor package owns the ProseMirror nodes, marks, plugins and commands; the React app mounts it directly on ProseMirror primitives (EditorView, L27) with an extension manager assembling the stack (ExtensionManager, L39).
  • Realtime is Hocuspocus, tuned and extended. Server.configure, L46 sets debounce to 3000 ms with a 30000 ms timeout, then chains eleven extensions — JWT auth, throttling, connection limits, awareness identity, persistence, API updates, views, logging, metrics.
  • The database is the source of truth, even live. PersistenceExtension, L21 hydrates each Y.Doc straight from the Postgres state column in onLoadDocument, and when state does not exist yet it converts stored ProseMirror content with toYDoc, L90 before persisting it in a transaction.
  • Attribution rides a Redis zset. afterLoadDocument, L119 hooks every document update and records the acting user with zaddWithSequence (zaddWithSequence, L136), so the eventual snapshot knows exactly who edited it.
  • Storing is a snapshot, not a stream. onStoreDocument, L165 encodes the document once with Y.encodeStateAsUpdate (L186) and hands it to documentCollaborativeUpdater (L221), retrying at most maxPersistFailures, L23 — five attempts — before giving up.
  • Background work is Bull on Redis. createQueue, L11 builds Bull queues over shared ioredis clients with stalled/completed/failed metrics; globalEventQueue, L5 is one of four named queues a dedicated worker drains.
  • The REST surface is resource-per-router. apiRouter, L57 composes roughly thirty resource routers — documents, revisions, searches, shares, stars, templates — behind koa-body parsing, CSRF verification and rate limiting.
  • Everything converges on the Document model. Document, L325 holds the content as ProseMirror JSONB (L426) and the Yjs state as a BLOB (L438), publishes domain events after commit, and pings the collaboration server on state changes (notifyCollaborationServer, L664).

Detail: the collaboration service with its extension chain, the Koa API layer over Sequelize models, the Postgres tsvector GIN index, the Bull queue and processor topology, and the SSO auth plugins.

One Codebase, Two Servers

The first thing to internalize is that Outline is two servers in one process tree. The web service is a plain Koa application: init, L25 builds the app and mounts the API, auth, oauth and MCP routers at app.use(mount(routes)), L110. The collaboration service attaches to the same HTTP server’s upgrade event at the /collaboration path (upgrade handler, L76) and hands each WebSocket to Hocuspocus. This Node.js pairing — synchronous REST for reads and writes, asynchronous WebSocket for typing — is the same two-channel pattern we documented in the Node source tour, applied here with a mature CRDT framework instead of hand-rolled messaging.

The extension chain is where Outline customizes Hocuspocus. AuthenticationExtension, L51 resolves the JWT during onAuthenticate (onAuthenticate, L77) and closes connections whose token has expired — the client simply reconnects with a fresh token. Connection limiting, throttling and editor-version checks sit in front, so a misbehaving client is rejected before it can touch a document.

How a Keystroke Becomes a Yjs Update

On the client, ProseMirror and Yjs are bound by the y-prosemirror plugins imported in Multiplayer, L4: the extension gets the shared Y.XmlFragment named default (doc.get, L51) and installs sync, cursor and undo plugins over it. Local edits become Yjs updates; remote updates become ProseMirror transactions. The extension also watches Yjs transactions to attribute each change to a client ID, which is what powers the collaborator badges in the UI.

On the server, the reverse conversion is the interesting part. When the last socket closes, onStoreDocument takes the snapshot and calls documentCollaborativeUpdater, which imports the same ProseMirror schema the editor uses (schema from @server/editor, documentCollaborativeUpdater, L8) and converts the Y.Doc back to ProseMirror JSON with yDocToProsemirrorJSON (L4). That is the trick that keeps one canonical content representation: the Yjs state is the live format, the JSONB column is the projection everyone renders, and ProsemirrorHelper, L150 provides toYDoc and toState, L169 to move between them.

One Postgres, Three Shapes of the Same Document

Outline’s data layer is deliberately boring and therefore worth copying. getDatabaseConfig, L33 hard-codes dialect: "postgres" (L46) — there is no MySQL mode, no pluggable ORM. Sequelize models map every resource, and the three representations of a document live in one documents table: content JSONB for rendering, state BLOB for collaborative continuity, and a searchVector tsvector column maintained by database triggers. The migration documents_team_id_tsv_idx, L10 builds a composite GIN index over (teamId, searchVector) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which is why full-text search stays fast at team scale — this is exactly the Postgres-native search strategy we covered in the Postgres source tour.

The wiki part of “team wiki” is the document tree, and it is a JSONB column too. documentStructure, L276 on the Collection model holds the NavigationNode[] hierarchy, and moving a document rewrites that structure in one place (updateCollectionStructure, L517) instead of shuffling foreign keys across rows. Revisions take a different route: the revisions table (Revision, L36) stores title and content snapshots with collaborator attribution, created asynchronously so typing never waits on history.

Redis Queues Turn Edits Into Revisions, Backlinks and Search

Every meaningful domain change is published as an event after the transaction commits: Event, L88 enqueues the model into globalEventQueue, one of four Bull queues defined in server/queues (global events, processor events, websocket pushes, tasks). The worker service (init, L18) consumes all four and dispatches each event by name to registered processors — the fan-out topology we described in the Redis source tour, but with event routing made explicit in code.

Three processors do most of the wiki housekeeping. RevisionsProcessor, L11 fires on debounced document updates, compares against the latest revision, skips no-op saves, and writes a snapshot through Revision.createFromDocument (L77) — this is why the revision list shows meaningful versions rather than every keystroke. BacklinksProcessor, L17 parses document links and maintains Relationship rows (L133) so “what links here” survives renames and deletes. SearchIndexProcessor, L21 is the interesting negative case: its shouldQueue returns false when the search provider is Postgres (L45), because the tsvector triggers already did the indexing — the queue only carries work for external providers.

From Notion Tabs to a Self-Hosted Wiki: Build Facts Worth Stealing

  • One shared editor package eliminates drift. The shared/editor directory is compiled once and consumed by both the React app and the server-side converters; documentCollaborativeUpdater reuses the identical schema for server rendering, so what users typed is what exports and previews show.
  • Boring storage wins. A single Postgres dialect, one documents table with JSONB plus BLOB plus tsvector, and GIN indexes built CONCURRENTLY — no second database to run until you truly need one.
  • Auth is a plugin folder. Google, Slack, OIDC, Azure, Discord, email and passkeys each live in plugins/<name>/server/auth; the auth router mounts whatever providers exist (auth routes, L97), so adding SSO means adding a folder, not patching a god file.
  • Debounce at the boundary, snapshot at the edge. Hocuspocus debounces 3 seconds and persists once per session end, with a five-attempt retry cap — durable writes without per-keystroke database load.
  • API and realtime write paths converge. REST edits call APIUpdateExtension.notifyUpdate through the Document model hook, and both paths end in documentCollaborativeUpdater, which means one place to enforce validation for every write.
  • Import and export are first-class endpoints. documents.import (documents.import, L1742) and documents.export, L933 make migration from Notion or Markdown a supported operation, processed through dedicated import queues rather than request handlers.

Honest Limits

  • Search beyond Postgres is opt-in and external. The built-in path is tsvector triggers; Elasticsearch-style providers require queue-driven indexing and a running external cluster — the code does not hide this (shouldQueue, L44).
  • Multi-process collaboration fan-out depends on configuration. The Hocuspocus Redis extension is only attached when REDIS_COLLABORATION_URL is set (conditional, L51); a single-instance deployment works without it, but cross-process socket sync needs that Redis.
  • Persistence is capped, not infinite. After five failed snapshot attempts the extension stops retrying that document until new edits arrive (giveUp branch, L237) — resilience by bounded retry, not by queueing writes.
  • Payload size is enforced at the socket. The WebSocket server caps documents at DocumentValidation.maxStateLength (maxPayload, L34) and tolerates oversized-payload errors instead of crashing the process.
  • Identical edits do not create revisions. When the new snapshot equals the previous revision, the processor returns early and clears the attribution zset (skip branch, L50) — revision history records content changes, not comment-only touches.
entry.summary: How Outline's self-hosted team wiki works internally: Koa API, ProseMirror editor, Yjs realtime sync, Postgres storage and search, Redis Bull queues, SSO auth.

entry.title: How SiYuan Works: Inside the Block-Based Note-Taking Kernel Architecture

link.title: How SiYuan Works: Inside the Block-Based Note-Taking Kernel Architecture

entry.content:
Most note apps treat a document as an opaque blob. A paragraph is just a fragment of one big markdown file, so “link to exactly this paragraph” degenerates into text search, “what references this heading” requires re-parsing your whole vault, and transcluding a block means copying text that silently drifts out of date. SiYuan makes the opposite bet: every paragraph, heading, list item, and table row is a first-class block with a stable ID, and the app indexes each one so you can reference, transclude, and query any paragraph the way you would query a database row.

That promise has to be delivered by architecture, not slogans. The two diagrams in this post map how it actually is delivered. The overview shows the shape of the system: an Electron shell and TypeScript editor talking to a Go kernel over HTTP and a WebSocket, with a SQLite index underneath and a snapshot-based sync layer on top. The detail diagram zooms into the write path — from a keystroke in the editor to a transaction, to a re-indexed document tree, to rows landing in the blocks, spans, and refs tables.

Reading the source with that map in hand teaches three concrete things: how a markdown-flavored document gets projected into addressable rows, why backlink queries stay fast without re-parsing files, and how SiYuan syncs content-addressed snapshots instead of shuffling raw files around. Every symbol and line number below is verified against the master branch of the siyuan-note/siyuan repository.

Overview of SiYuan: the TypeScript frontend and the Go kernel meet at one HTTP/WebSocket boundary; all writes funnel through the transaction engine into the SQLite index.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • One process boots everything. The kernel’s main, L15 only runs a cobra command; the serve subcommand calls server.Serve, L61 in a goroutine and InitDatabase, L62 on the main one. Electron then just points a BrowserWindow at 127.0.0.1.
  • The server is gin with strict middleware. Serve, L130 builds a gin engine that serializes requests (ControlConcurrency, L144), then registers assets, WebDAV, MCP, and the API (ServeAPI, L184).
  • The editor is a browser view, not a native shell. The Protyle, L127 class opens a WebSocket per document via new WebSocket, L81 against the kernel’s /ws endpoint (serveWebSocket, L1885).
  • Writes arrive as ordered transactions. The editor batches DOM edits and posts them to /api/transactions (fetchPost, L752), where PerformTransactions, L210 replays them server-side — the client never writes SQLite directly.
  • Documents persist as JSON trees. Full indexing loads every .sy file (the suffix check, L278), parses it with the Lute engine, and queues rows via IndexTreeQueue, L641.
  • Every block is a table row. The schema at CREATE TABLE blocks, L179 stores id, parent_id, root_id, hash, box, path, content, markdown, and type per block — the Block struct, L26 mirrors it.
  • Row identity is content-hashed. Each block gets a 7-hex digest computed from its markdown, IAL attributes, and parent (sha256 slice, L55), so identical content produces identical hashes.
  • Search is FTS5 external content. blocks_fts, L332 is a virtual table whose rowids are shared with blocks, giving full-text search without duplicating storage ownership.
  • Backlinks come from a refs table. The refs schema, L284 stores def-block/ref-block pairs; GetBacklink2, L614 turns those rows into the backlink panel in one indexed query.

The detail view: boot chain and transport on top, the model layer in the middle, the SQLite writers at the bottom left, sync and the bazaar on the right.

Why a Go kernel sits behind an Electron window

SiYuan’s packaging is unusual: it ships an Electron desktop app, but the app is mostly a thin shell. The TypeScript side (over two thousand .ts files, zero .vue files — this is plain TypeScript with webpack, package.json, L2) renders tabs, panels, and the Protyle editor, while all state lives in the Go process. That split is what makes block-level features coherent: whether you edit from the desktop app, the browser when serving over the network, or a mobile client, the same kernel serializes writes and broadcasts changes.

The WebSocket is not a nice-to-have; it is the state channel. When the server’s handleWebSocketMessage, L2002 receives a message, it dispatches to session-scoped handlers that push events like document reloads, sync status, and bazaar changes back to every listening tab. The overview’s long edge from the SQLite store back to the editor is exactly this: the editor re-renders from server-pushed state instead of maintaining its own truth. If you want to compare this client-server split with other runtimes, the Go and Node source tours on this blog cover the two most common alternatives.

The write path: keystroke to indexed row

Follow one edit through the detail diagram. The editor computes a diff of your change and serializes it as an operation — insert, update, move, delete of a specific block ID — then POSTs the batch. The route lives in the API router (registerTransactionsRoutes, L716), and the model layer replays the operations in order (PerformTransactions, L210) against the in-memory tree before enqueueing the affected document for re-index.

Re-indexing is differential, not full-scan. The queued tree lands in upsertTreeWithChanges, L441, which writes only the rows that actually changed, and each AST node is projected into its row by buildBlockFromNode, L1000 — filling content, markdown, parent and root IDs in one pass. Inline elements go through buildSpanFromNode, L800: every tag, image, and block-ref TextMark becomes a row in spans (Span struct, L33), which is how SiYuan can list “all blocks with tags” or “all images” without scanning text.

The same pass maintains the link graph. Block references become pairs in refs via upsertRefs, L28, keyed by the definition block they point at. That is the trick behind backlinks and mentions: RefreshBacklink, L28 recomputes per-document, and queries like GetBacklinkDoc, L262 join the refs table against the blocks table — indexed lookups instead of full-text scans. This is the same insight that relational SQLite designs exploit everywhere: precompute relationships at write time so reads stay cheap.

Blocks, trees, and seven-hex-char hashes

Storage has three layers that many people conflate. On disk, a document is one .sy file — a JSON serialization of the block tree — named after its root block ID; the rename logic that keeps file name and root ID in lockstep appends the ID to the path (the .sy path join, L68). In memory, the tree is a Lute AST (SiYuan’s markdown engine, imported at tree.go, L17). In the index, the same tree is rows in blocks with parent/child and root columns rebuilt from the AST hierarchy.

The hash column deserves attention because it encodes identity, not just checksums. NodeHashWithHeadingParent, L31 digests the notebook and path, the sorted IAL attributes, the formatted markdown, and the parent ID, then keeps the first 7 hex characters of the sha256. Change any of those inputs and the hash changes, which lets the index detect real edits cheaply and lets history views tell “you retyped it” from “nothing changed”. The full-text index rides along: blocks_fts is declared with content='blocks' (FTS5 virtual table, L332), so the tokenizer reads straight from the blocks table by rowid rather than owning a second copy of the text — and the schema comment notes the tokenizer is fixed at creation time, so changing tokenization requires an explicit rebuild.

From Markdown blobs to SQLite rows: build facts

A few verified facts for anyone building on top of this stack. The kernel is a single Go module: SQLite through mattn/go-sqlite3 with a registered sqlite3_extended driver (sql.Register, L67), routing through gin, WebSockets through melody (melody.New, L1886), markdown through 88250/lute, and sync through siyuan-note/dejavu (imported at repository.go, L37). The frontend is Electron 44 with TypeScript and webpack (electron, L85), building desktop, mobile, and export bundles from the same sources. Historically this codebase migrated from a Python-free pure-frontend design into today’s split: documents that used to be loose markdown files became .sy JSON trees, and text indexes that used to be ad-hoc became the FTS5-backed blocks projection — the direction of travel is always “make the block addressable”. The API surface is stable enough that plugins, and the bazaar listing at GetUpdatedPackages, L211, can extend the kernel without forking it.

Sync: snapshot deltas over four providers

Sync is built on snapshots, not file copies. The kernel wraps the dejavu engine (repository.go exposes snapshot listing, diffing, and rollback at GetRepoSnapshots, L1061), and SyncData, L272 drives boot-time, scheduled, and manual syncs through one path. The provider switch is explicit in config: official cloud (ProviderSiYuan), S3-compatible object storage, WebDAV, and a local filesystem provider (provider constants, L71); SetSyncProvider, L699 validates the endpoint before committing. Because the units of transfer are content-addressed snapshot files, the same mechanism serves version history and rollback — restoring a document is a checkout, not a “recently edited files” heuristic. Conflicts are detected rather than last-write-wins, and the WebSocket pushes sync state so open tabs react when another device changes the workspace.

Honest Limits

  • The SQLite index is a projection, not the source of truth. The .sy files remain canonical; the kernel even skips indexing encrypted notebooks entirely (the encrypted-box guard, L143), so encrypted content is searchable only after decryption.
  • The block hash is truncated to 7 hex characters (L55). It is a change-detection key, not a cryptographic guarantee against collisions.
  • The FTS5 tokenizer is fixed when blocks_fts is created (L332); switching case sensitivity or tokenization requires a rebuild, it is not a live setting.
  • refs rows are built during indexing (upsertRefs, L28), so external tools editing .sy files on disk will not appear in backlinks until the kernel re-indexes them.
  • Request serialization is deliberate: the kernel processes API requests one at a time (ControlConcurrency, L144), trading throughput for consistency on a single-user desktop workload.
entry.summary: Inside SiYuan's Go kernel: how notes become SQLite block rows, how transactions, backlinks and FTS5 search work, and how snapshot sync keeps notebooks current.

entry.title: How Domoticz Works: Inside the Open-Source Home Automation Server

link.title: How Domoticz Works: Inside the Open-Source Home Automation Server

entry.content:
Two hundred sensors report into one box. Zigbee door contacts, 433 MHz motion detectors, a MySensors temperature node on a battery, an HTTP weather poller — all of it converges on a single Domoticz process, and the dashboard keeps updating every few seconds. Then device #201 joins the mesh, scripts start firing late, and the usual “fix” is a nightly reboot and hope. If you have run a home automation server at any scale, you know exactly the afternoon this describes.

The reason Domoticz survives that kind of load is not magic, it is a specific and slightly unusual core design: every incoming sensor message crosses exactly two worker threads and one queue before it becomes a dashboard dot. Hardware adapters never touch the database. The database update is what triggers your Lua scripts — not the hardware, not the web layer. Once you see that separation, the whole repository reads like a well-rehearsed relay race.

We read the development branch line by line and traced one temperature reading from a serial gateway all the way to a fired script. Every claim below links into the real source on GitHub, and both diagrams were generated from the actual tree. If you want a comparable walkthrough of the interpreter that powers Domoticz’s plugin system, our CPython source tour covers that side.

Domoticz at a glance: one process, two worker threads, and everything speaking through queues, signals and one SQLite file.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process starts in main() at domoticz.cpp, L676, parses command line and config, installs SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers, and hands everything to m_mainworker.Start() at domoticz.cpp, L1241.
  • MainWorker::Start, L1136 fixes the startup order: database first (L1147), plugin system (L1158), hardware adapters (L1160), web servers (L1181).
  • Startup ends by spawning two threads: the main heartbeat loop (L1262) and a dedicated RX-message thread (L1264).
  • Every hardware adapter derives from CDomoticzHardwareBase, L13 and reports through one shared signal, sDecodeRXMessage at DomoticzHardware.h, L52.
  • The RX queue thread pops frames in Do_Work_On_Rx_Messages, L2016 and dispatches them into the giant protocol switch in ProcessRXMessage, L2098.
  • Decoded devices land in SQLite through CSQLHelper::UpdateValue, L5280, which delegates to UpdateValueInt, L5892.
  • The database update hands off to the event engine at SQLHelper.cpp, L5680, where ProcessDevice, L1644 queues work for Lua and dzVents scripts.
  • The web front-end binds its ports in CWebServer::StartServer, L153 and registers every /json.htm command via RegisterCommandCode, L354.
  • Python plugins are optional at build time; they are started only when ENABLE_PYTHON is compiled in (mainworker.cpp, L1158).

The detail view follows one message through the decoders, the SQL write, the event queue and back out through the web command table.

One hub, two worker threads, one RX queue

The design decision that keeps a 200-device hub responsive is deceptively small: hardware adapters are never allowed to process inline. When any adapter has a frame, it fires the sDecodeRXMessage signal — for example SendTempSensor, L179 packs a temperature struct and fires the signal with a byte buffer. MainWorker connected its own slot to that signal at startup (mainworker.cpp, L356), and the slot does almost nothing: DecodeRXMessage, L1891 pushes the raw bytes into a lock-free-ish concurrent_queue and returns. A chatty serial gateway can therefore produce messages as fast as the port delivers them without ever blocking on SQL.

The RX thread is where the real work happens. Do_Work_On_Rx_Messages, L2016 waits up to five seconds per pop, resolves the hardware object by id, then calls ProcessRXMessage (L2088). That function is a switch on the protocol byte at mainworker.cpp, L2110 — Lighting2, blinds, wind meters, security sensors, dozens of decoders, each one converting the raw buffer into device values. Only after a decoder succeeds does the worker announce the device by firing its own sOnDeviceReceived signal at mainworker.cpp, L2370 — which is exactly how the MQTT hardware, for instance, re-broadcasts updates (MQTT.cpp, L188). Inbound and outbound device changes share a funnel: the outbound path used by JSON commands, MainWorker::UpdateDevice, L14482, ultimately writes through the same SQL helper the RX thread uses.

There is one documented exception to the queue rule: shared “Domoticz-to-Domoticz” hardware with id 8765 decodes inline under a mutex (mainworker.cpp, L1895). Everything else queues.

Hardware: one base class, 149 adapters

Open the hardware/ folder and you find 149 .cpp files: RFXCOM serial and TCP, MySensors serial/MQTT/TCP, MQTT auto-discovery, Philips Hue, OpenZWave, an HTTP poller, and subfolders for 1-Wire, eHouse, openwebnet and others. All of them are small variations on one contract. CDomoticzHardwareBase gives each adapter a heartbeat thread (DomoticzHardware.cpp, L106), logging helpers, and about forty typed Send* methods that translate device semantics into the internal byte format. An adapter’s Start() spawns its own worker thread — see MySensorsSerial, L35 spawning its thread at L48 — and pushes bytes upward through the base-class signal.

Pull-style devices use the same contract in reverse. CHttpPoller has no serial line; its Do_Work, L76 loop fetches a URL on a timer and pushes the parsed values upward, so the rest of the system cannot tell whether a reading arrived by RF or by HTTP. The serial transport itself is a separate reusable layer: the AsyncSerial class at ASyncSerial.h, L26 with a setReadCallback hook that MySensors wires to its readCallback, L190, which parses node messages and calls SendSensor2Domoticz, L602 to emit typed sensors.

The plugin system sits on top of the same base class. CPluginSystem::StartPluginSystem, L82 boots an embedded CPython interpreter (the Py_Initialize call is at PluginManager.cpp, L153), and each Python plugin.py becomes a CPlugin — a hardware adapter — with its own message-pump thread (Plugins.cpp, L1225) draining command objects derived from CPluginMessageBase, L17. If you want to understand what Py_Initialize actually spins up, the CPython internals tour is the natural companion.

SQLite is the middle of the bus

Every decoded value, every timer tick, every JSON write ends in one place: CSQLHelper. The database opens first thing in startup (SQLHelper.cpp, L711) and owns the DeviceStatus table plus the shortlog tables that power the graphs. UpdateValue at SQLHelper.cpp, L5280 is the funnel: it resolves the device row by hardware/device-id/unit/type, inserts a fresh row on first sighting via InsertDevice, L5518, and finally delegates to UpdateValueInt, L5892, which updates DeviceStatus, refreshes logs and emits sOnDeviceReceived (the emit used by shared-user propagation is at SQLHelper.cpp, L11747).

The line that matters most for scripting is SQLHelper.cpp, L5680: only for devices marked as used, UpdateValueInt calls m_eventsystem.ProcessDevice(...). That single call means the event engine is downstream of the database, not of the hardware. A device that is not “used” never triggers scripts at all — a Domoticz gotcha that is obvious once you read this line and invisible otherwise. We traced the storage engine itself in the SQLite source tour if you want to know what happens underneath these calls.

The event engine: Lua, dzVents, and a 12-second heartbeat

CEventSystem::ProcessDevice at EventSystem.cpp, L1644 is the event gate. It first dedupes: for non-switch devices, an unchanged value only refreshes lastUpdate and returns (L1665) — a deliberate guard against faulty sensors that transmit ten times a second. Real changes get wrapped into _tEventQueue items and drained by the event thread started at StartEventSystem, L154. That worker (Do_Work, L350) does something unusual: it sleeps until the next multiple of twelve seconds (L381) so time-based scripts run on coarse, predictable boundaries, then handles minute-based logic on the minute.

Script execution has two layers. Classic Lua scripts run through EvaluateLuaClassic, L2894 inside a dedicated lua_State, with a watchdog thread (luaThread at L3377) so a looping script cannot hang the engine. Before any script runs, ExportDeviceStatesToLua, L2849 materialises all device states as Lua tables via the table builder at LuaTable.cpp, L23 — that is what makes domoticz.devices() work. dzVents is the friendlier layer on top, versioned in-code at dzVents.cpp, L47 (3.1.13) and routed through EvaluateDzVents, L56. There is no Python event path in this default flow — Python is reserved for the plugin system.

The same funnel serves the front door. The UI is a separate app under www/; what it talks to is a flat JSON command table. CWebServer::StartServer, L153 binds the HTTP and SSL ports (the accept loop lives in Do_Work at L102), and startup registers dozens of commands with RegisterCommandCode, L354 — each entry maps one /json.htm command name to a Cmd_* handler plus a minimum user-rights level. Cmd_GetVersion (WebServerCmds.cpp, L2695) is what the login screen probes first; the dashboard’s device list is Cmd_GetDevices, L4834.
