Control commands funnel into MainWorker::UpdateDevice, so a web click follows the same SQL and event path as an RF message — there is no ORM or request-object layer anywhere near what a Django app gives you, just functions that end in SQL.

From CMake 3.16 to a 15k-line worker: build facts

Measured on the development branch, the build is refreshingly explicit. The floor is CMake 3.16 (CMakeLists.txt, L2) with C++17 required (L64). Dependencies are pinned in text: Boost must be at least 1.69 (L16), Lua 5.3 is a hard requirement — the configure step literally tells you to apt-get install liblua5.3-dev if it is missing (L501) — and OpenSSL is REQUIRED (L673). SQLite can be either the system package or the bundled amalgamation behind the USE_BUILTIN_SQLITE option (L26), which refuses to configure without extern/sqlite-amalgamation present (L157). Plugin support needs the Python 3 development component (L512) and is otherwise compiled out.

The size distribution tells you where the project’s complexity actually lives: main/mainworker.cpp is 14,999 lines in this tree, main/SQLHelper.cpp is 12,623, and main/EventSystem.cpp is 4,775 — the hub, the storage funnel and the event engine are deliberately three huge files rather than many small ones. Versioning is date-based: appversion.h defines VERSION_MAJOR 2026, VERSION_MINOR 4 (appversion.h, L8), and this branch reports the beta channel (L17). The default branch here is development, not main — worth knowing before you cite line numbers.

Honest Limits

  • The plugin system is compile-time optional. Everything in the plugin section is guarded by #ifdef ENABLE_PYTHON (mainworker.cpp, L1158); a build without Python has no plugins at all.
  • One hardware type skips the queue: shared Domoticz hardware (id 8765) decodes inline under a mutex (mainworker.cpp, L1895), so the “everything queues” claim has this one carve-out.
  • Only used devices trigger events (SQLHelper.cpp, L5680); unused devices are stored but script-silent.
  • We traced dzVents only at its entry points (dzVents.cpp, L56); the user-facing dzVents framework files live in the top-level dzVents/ directory and were not covered here.
  • The www/ front-end application (its JS app, themes and templates) is out of scope; we covered only the JSON command layer it consumes.
  • Line numbers and file sizes were measured against the development branch head at publication time; this is an active branch and they will drift.
entry.summary: Trace one sensor message through Domoticz's open-source home automation server: RX queue, SQLite device store, Lua event engine, and the JSON API.

entry.title: How ESPHome Works: Inside the Compiler That Turns YAML into ESP32 Firmware

link.title: How ESPHome Works: Inside the Compiler That Turns YAML into ESP32 Firmware

entry.content:
You type esphome run device.yaml, wait about a minute, and the ESP32 on your desk is blinking. Two hundred lines of indentation-sensitive text went in; a megabyte of Xtensa machine code came out. Between those two moments there is no magic — there is a compiler: a Python program that validates your YAML against hundreds of schemas, translates every component into C++ objects, and hands the result to a real cross-toolchain.

The folklore says ESPHome “converts YAML into firmware” and stops there. That hides the interesting part: the intermediate representation. ESPHome does not paste your YAML into string templates. Each component’s to_code coroutine builds typed expression objects — variable declarations, calls, lambdas — that only get rendered to source text at the very end, so the tool knows which IDs point at which objects before a single line of C++ exists.

We read that compiler path in the repository’s own source to see exactly where your 200 lines go: the validation gauntlet, the code generation flow, the fixed setup()/loop() skeleton everything gets spliced into, and the protobuf-based native API the finished firmware speaks. Every claim below links to the file and line we verified.

ESPHome at a glance: YAML in, validated config, generated main.cpp, toolchain build, and a device runtime that serves the native API and accepts OTA updates.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Your YAML is parsed by yaml_util, which wraps secrets in a Sensitive type so keys never leak into logs or generated code.
  • read_config, L1778 is the entry point that loads and validates the file, returning None with a formatted error instead of a config.
  • validate_config, L1287 runs substitutions and packages first, then a priority-ordered queue of validation passes.
  • SchemaValidationStep, L986 checks every domain block against its CONFIG_SCHEMA via voluptuous schemas.
  • iter_component_configs, L62 yields each validated (domain, manifest, config) triple, expanding per-platform entries.
  • generate_cpp_contents, L812 schedules one to_code job per component and flushes the task queue.
  • Pvariable, L791 and add build the C++ expression tree that becomes your device objects.
  • write_cpp, L534 splices the rendered code into CPP_BASE_FORMAT, L39, the skeleton whose setup() calls App.setup().
  • compile_program, L849 dispatches to the ESP-IDF or PlatformIO backend; the flashed firmware runs Application::setup, L144.

The detail view: the validation passes, the expression-object code generator, the two toolchain backends, and the API/OTA stacks your binary ships with.

Validation: your YAML runs a gauntlet, not a schema check

validate_config is not one pass but a queue of ConfigValidationStep objects executed in priority order. Substitutions and packages are resolved first (config.py, steps 0 and 1 in the source), then auto-loads pull in dependencies each component declares, then the schema pass, then an ID pass, then cross-component final validation. A block like sensor: with a platform: dht entry is loaded, its platform manifest is resolved, and only then is the block handed to that platform’s schema.

The schema engine is voluptuous — All, L165 and Any subclass the library’s own combinators — but ESPHome layers real semantics on top: templatable() marks options that accept both literal values and runtime lambdas, update_interval() accepts 60s or 1min and returns a normalized time period, and validators like mac_address or ssid encode hardware rules in plain Python. If you have read our tour of CPython’s compiler internals, this will feel familiar: a parse tree refined pass by pass, except here the “ast” is your YAML dict with source ranges attached, which is why an invalid option reports the exact file and line you typed.

The ID pass deserves its own sentence: IDPassValidationStep, L1024 is where id: my_sensor references get bound. Automatic IDs are assigned when omitted, duplicates are rejected, and every cross-reference is checked to point at a declared object of the right type — before code generation, so a typo fails with a message, not a C++ compile error three layers deep.

The last pass is the only one that sees the whole device: FinalValidateValidationStep, L1215 runs each component’s cross-domain hook. This is where the OTA platform reconciles two ota: blocks that share a port, merges them, and refuses inconsistent encryption keys — checks that are impossible for any single schema, because they involve other domains’ config.

Code generation: every component becomes a C++ stanza

Code generation starts from the validated config, not your raw YAML. generate_cpp_contents, L812 walks iter_component_configs and adds one job per component that defines to_code. Each coroutine receives the validated dict for its domain and emits C++ through the cpp_generator expression classes: new_Pvariable declares an object, cg.add(var.set_port(...)) records a method call, process_lambda turns your YAML lambda into a real C++ lambda. These are objects with types and dependencies, not strings — that is how the generator knows a GPIOPin expression can be passed where a pin is expected.

One delightfully practical detail: _wrap_to_code, L772 wraps every to_code so the original YAML block lands in main.cpp as a comment right above the code it produced. The wrapper dumps the config with sort_keys=True — the comment explains that an unsorted dump would churn main.cpp and relink the firmware on every run even when nothing changed.

The accumulated statements land in CORE.cpp_main_section, and write_cpp_file, L829 hands them to the writer. Generation is not strictly sequential, either: each to_code is registered as a job on CORE via add_job, L1081 and flushed as a batch, so domains can emit in dependency order while ID references stay consistent. write_cpp reads the existing src/main.cpp, keeps whatever human-written sections live between the AUTO GENERATED markers, and splices in the new code — so you can edit the generated file’s outer regions and your edits survive the next esphome run. Lambdas get #line directives pointing back at your YAML, reset after each one by _reset_line_directives, L515, so a compiler error inside a lambda cites the YAML line you wrote.

From 200 lines of YAML to a 1 MB binary: build facts

The dev branch we read builds version 2026.12.0-dev (const.py, L7); the package targets Python 3.12–3.15. The core toolchain dependencies are pinned hard in requirements.txt: voluptuous 0.16.0, PyYAML 6.0.3, platformio 6.2.0, and esptool 5.6.0 for serial flashing. The component library is enormous — 866 directories under esphome/components/ — yet a minimal build compiles only the domains your YAML names, because generation is demand-driven from the validated config.

Compilation itself is dispatched per platform. ESP32/ESP-IDF builds go through espidf’s run_compile, L860, which drives idf.py and then produces factory and OTA images; Arduino/ESP8266 builds go through platformio’s run_compile, L369. A quirk worth knowing: writer.py has drifted from its name — today it is build-directory management (storage, cleaning, source-tree copying), and the actual main.cpp emission lives in __main__.py plus that one write_cpp function. Another: api_pb2.cpp, the protobuf codec, is committed to the repo but machine-generated — its header points at script/api_protobuf/api_protobuf.py, so editing wire messages by hand in the .proto alone is not enough.

The compile is also deliberately incremental: main.cpp is only recompiled when the configuration actually changed, as coroutine.py’s header, L15 spells out — generated code changes rarely, so the expensive C++ link is skipped on no-op runs. If you enjoy systems built as compiler plus codegen like this, our tour of Rust’s build architecture covers the other end of the trade: slower iteration, stronger runtime guarantees.

The runtime: App.setup() and the component contract

The firmware you flash has a tiny, boring entry point. The skeleton from CPP_BASE_FORMAT, L39 defines setup() that calls App.setup() and loop() that calls App.loop() — everything else is the framework. Application::setup walks every registered component in setup-priority order, calling its setup(), which is where a sensor reads its first value or Wi-Fi associates. Then App.loop() iterates the same component list forever; a Component is just virtual setup and loop, L154 plus an update interval and a status flag.

That contract is why the YAML vanishes at runtime. Nothing in the flashed binary parses configuration; every if your YAML expressed became a C++ conditional or a define compiled in (USE_OTA_ENCRYPTION, USE_API_HOMEASSISTANT_SERVICES, and friends are emitted during code generation). The cost is that behavior is fixed at build time; the benefit is a loop deterministic enough to run on 80 KB of RAM — and it is why two devices whose YAMLs differ compile to different binaries even from the same ESPHome version.

Talking to hubs: the native API and OTA

The api component is what makes the device a first-class citizen of Home Assistant. Its to_code, L584 registers the server, then emits defines for connection limits, batching delays, and the services you exposed. The wire format is protobuf over TCP, defined in api.proto, L111: a HelloRequest opens every connection, ListEntitiesRequest discovers what the device offers, and SubscribeStatesRequest, L558 streams state changes forever. The C++ codec in api_pb2.cpp is pre-generated, and each client gets an APIConnection object dispatching frames. If your hub is Domoticz rather than Home Assistant, there is no native API client yet — the practical bridge is MQTT, which we cover in our Domoticz setup tour.

OTA is a stack of two components. The shared ota base defines the component and its per-platform flash backends; the ota/esphome platform (to_code, L366) compiles in the protocol specifics: noise encryption keys shared with the API component, deflate for compressed uploads, and the response codes you can read in OTAResponseTypes, L18. The uploading side lives in the CLI at espota2.py, L33, with default ports per platform and the handshake state machine that probes a device before pushing an image.

Honest Limits

  • Everything here reads the dev branch at commit 904f0df (version 2026.12.0-dev). ESPHome moves fast; line numbers will drift, and some of these functions will be renamed by release.
  • We verified code, not hardware: no ESP32 was flashed for this post. The host platform can build and run the same generated program locally, but we did not execute it either.
  • The protobuf generation script (script/api_protobuf/) was not in our sparse checkout; the claim that api_pb2.cpp is generated comes from the generated file’s own header comment.
  • Toolchain acquisition (ESP-IDF downloads, PlatformIO packages) happens outside this repository, so version resolution of the actual compilers is not visible in the code we read.
  • The 866-component count and dependency pins are facts of the dev tree at read time; released versions differ.
entry.summary: Follow esphome run device.yaml through validation, C++ code generation, and the ESP32 toolchain build — read straight from the ESPHome compiler source.

entry.title: How Frigate NVR Works: Inside the Real-Time Camera AI Architecture

link.title: How Frigate NVR Works: Inside the Real-Time Camera AI Architecture

entry.content:
Every camera vendor wants a subscription. Nest, Ring, and their imitators all work the same way: pay monthly, or your “smart” camera stops being smart — and either way, every person detection runs on somebody else’s servers, so full-motion video of your driveway, hallway, and front door routinely leaves your network. Frigate inverts that deal. It is a self-hosted network video recorder that runs real-time object detection on hardware you already own — a CPU, a Coral Edge TPU, an Intel iGPU via OpenVINO, or an NVIDIA Jetson via TensorRT — and publishes events over MQTT that Home Assistant turns into automations. No account, no monthly fee, no third-party server.

This post is a guided tour of the actual source tree (the dev branch, commit 7fd81171f0b35bfe), with two diagrams generated directly from the repository. The overview diagram traces the ten moving parts that carry one frame from an RTSP stream to a Home Assistant event. The detail diagram goes a level deeper: the detector plugin contract, the shared-memory frame store, the watchdogs that keep it all alive, and the communicator layer that talks to your browser and your MQTT broker.

By the end you will know why Frigate runs cheap motion detection before expensive object detection, how a single accelerator serves every camera without duplicating GPU processes, where the fixed-size detection result arrays live, and what the MQTT contract between Frigate and Home Assistant looks like in code.

Frigate overview: capture → shared memory → per-camera analysis → detector processes → tracking → events → MQTT/API. Every node links to the exact source file on the dev branch.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • CameraCapture, L765 is one process per camera. It does not decode video in Python at all — ffmpeg handles RTSP, and Frigate reads raw YUV frames from ffmpeg’s stdout pipe.
  • capture_frames, L49 is the hot loop: readinto() fills a shared-memory slot directly (L88), then pushes (frame_name, timestamp) onto a queue with a non-blocking put (L111). If the queue is full, the frame is skipped (L112–115) rather than ever back-pressuring ffmpeg.
  • SharedMemoryFrameManager, L1063 is the reason those names mean anything: every frame lives in a named slot in /dev/shm, so capture, tracking, recording, and output all read the same bytes with zero copying.
  • CameraTracker, L116 is the per-camera analysis process, and process_frames, L242 is its main loop. This is where motion detection, region selection, inference requests, and object matching happen.
  • ImprovedMotionDetector, L15 runs first on every frame (detect.py L375). Frame differencing costs microseconds; running a neural network on the full frame would cost orders of magnitude more.
  • RemoteObjectDetector, L410 is the client half of inference: it copies a cropped region tensor into shared memory (L455), puts its slot name on the detection queue (L456), and blocks on a ZMQ notification that the result is ready (L457). Frames never travel through the queue — only a short name string.
  • ObjectDetectProcess, L327 owns one accelerator. Many cameras enqueue into it; it processes requests one at a time on the device it controls.
  • api_types, L29 is the plugin registry: every DetectionApi subclass is collected at import time and indexed by its config type string, so adding a detector is a matter of subclassing, not editing core code.
  • MqttClient, L39 publishes on a worker thread (publish, L83). When the broker is down, retained publishes are queued in memory (L88–92) and flushed on reconnect — Home Assistant never sees a missed state flip.

The detail view: detector plugins and their per-device runtime, the two watchdog layers, frame analysis internals, event and review processes, communicators, recording, and the web stack.

The Startup Order Is the Architecture

FrigateApp.start() reads like a table of contents for the whole system, and the order is deliberate. Detectors come first: start_detectors, L393 pre-creates the per-camera input and output shared-memory blocks (a fixed 20×6 float32 result buffer per camera, L405–407), then builds one ObjectDetectProcess per configured accelerator (L426), each configured by build_detector_config, L61, which parses a device string — a /dev/apex_0 path, a PCI slot, a /dev/dri/renderD128 render node — into a concrete plugin config.

Then the service layer boots: the dispatcher (L686), video output (L696), the tracked-object processor (L698), and finally start_camera_processor, L461, which hands each camera to CameraMaintainer, L29. The maintainer starts a capture process (its __start_camera_capture at L154 pre-creates ten frame slots per camera at L164–167) and a tracker process per camera. Only after all of that does create_fastapi_app, L69 get served by uvicorn on 127.0.0.1:5001 (L718, L735–736) behind nginx.

Two watchdog layers keep this alive. FrigateWatchdog, L42 restarts any registered process through its factory (L101–102), and separately checks whether a detector has been stuck mid-inference for over ten seconds — if so it calls start_or_restart() (L122–126). Inside each capture process, CameraWatchdog, L141 watches frame staleness and restarts ffmpeg when a stream stalls.

Why Motion Detection Runs Before Object Detection

The core cost asymmetry of video AI is this: frame differencing is nearly free, neural inference is not. Frigate exploits it ruthlessly. In process_frames, the very first thing that happens to a decoded frame is motion_detector.detect(frame) — ImprovedMotionDetector, L15 computes motion boxes with pixel-level differencing, supporting masks and a calibration period on startup.

Those motion boxes, merged with the boxes of already-tracked objects, become detection regions: get_cluster_region consolidates candidates into a handful of rectangles sized against the model’s minimum region (L423–430). Standalone motion outside existing regions gets its own grid-informed regions (L443–465), and a startup scan sweeps the full frame once (L467–473). Only then does Frigate run detect() per region (L490–501): crop, resize to model input, infer, and map boxes back to full-frame coordinates (L221–224), then merge overlapping detections with reduce_detections (L503) and hand everything to the tracker via match_and_update (L511). This is why an idle Frigate with live cameras sits at near-zero CPU: full inference runs only when something moved.

One Detector Process, Many Cameras

The most economical trick in the codebase is detector sharing. app.py L111 creates one mp.Queue per model “scene”; every camera configured with that model drops its requests into the same queue. Each accelerator runs exactly one DetectorRunner, L133: its run loop (L159) pulls a connection id, map_input_frame, L116 turns that name into the tensor, detect_raw runs the plugin (L188), and the fixed-size result block — up to 20 detections, each 6 floats — is written straight into the requesting camera’s output shared memory (L194) before a ZMQ ping wakes the waiting camera (L195).

No frame data is ever pickled through a multiprocessing queue; the queue carries a camera-name string, and the heavy bytes move through shared memory. For accelerators that queue requests internally, there is an asynchronous variant, AsyncDetectorRunner, L204, which splits submission and result collection into separate worker threads (_detect_worker at L234). The tracker side keeps identity across frames with NorfairTracker, L115, combining centroid motion with histogram appearance (frigate_distance, L86). If you want to understand why these multiprocessing queues and shared-memory blocks behave the way they do under the hood, we’ve covered the foundations in our CPython internals deep dive.

From Docker Image to Detector Plugin

The build system mirrors the runtime plugin split. The docker/ directory is effectively a matrix of accelerator images: the base docker/main/Dockerfile plus build_ov_model.py and requirements-ov.txt for Intel OpenVINO targets; docker/tensorrt/Dockerfile.amd64 and Dockerfile.arm64 for Jetson; dedicated images for Rockchip (RKNN), ROCm, Raspberry Pi, and Synaptics; and user_installation.sh scripts for Hailo, Memryx, and DeepX boards. At runtime the choice is pure data — api_types collects all DetectionApi subclasses at import time (detector_types.py, L29), so the plugin file just needs to exist and subclass.

The current tree ships 14 plugin files. The ones most people run: CpuTfl, L41 on tflite-runtime for CPU-only boxes; EdgeTpuTfl, L40 for the Coral USB/PCIe TPU; OvDetector, L37 with dedicated YOLO post-processing (process_yolo at L142) for Intel iGPUs; and TensorRtDetector, L85, which allocates explicit GPU host/device buffers and runs _do_inference (L194) for NVIDIA. The web UI is a separate Vite + React app (web/src/App.tsx, with Live, Events, Explore, and Settings pages) that talks to the FastAPI backend and to WebSocket streams from api/ws.ts; live video itself is proxied by go2rtc, installed into the image by docker/main/install_go2rtc.sh.

Events, Review Segments, and the Home Assistant Contract

Once tracking produces a stable object, the event machinery takes over. Each camera’s tracker feeds detected_frames_queue into TrackedObjectProcessor, L58 — the central thread that decides which frames become snapshots (should_save_snapshot at L270), which become MQTT snapshot payloads (L317), and which become manually created events (L570). EventProcessor, L69 persists event start/end rows into SQLite — and on boot closes any event left open by a crash (L87–89). In parallel, ReviewProcess, L14 builds review segments that power the UI timeline, and RecordProcess, L17 writes recording segments for playback and export.

Everything user-visible leaves through Dispatcher, L63, the switchboard between Frigate internals and its communicators. Its publish (L490) fans object updates, stats, and review segments out to MqttClient and WebSocketClient, L582; inbound MQTT commands for the ~20 camera settings it registers (L93–115) flow back the other way, including live config changes like toggling detection or editing masks without restarts. The MQTT contract Home Assistant relies on is simple: every topic is prefixed (mqtt.py L85), availability and camera states are published retained, and if the broker drops, retained messages are queued and replayed on reconnect. That retained-topic pattern is exactly what makes zero-config discovery work in Home Assistant — and it is the same pattern you can reuse to wire Frigate events into Node-RED flows for automations, or into Domoticz event scripts if that is your hub of choice.

Honest Limits

  • Single host by design. The zero-copy frame store lives in /dev/shm; the capture, analysis, and detection processes must share one machine. There is no distributed mode in this codebase.
  • The API is not meant to be exposed. uvicorn binds 127.0.0.1:5001 (app.py L735–736) and expects nginx in front for TLS and auth. Pointing a browser at the Python port directly bypasses that design.
  • CPU detection is the floor, not the target. CpuTfl works, but the entire motion-first region design exists because full-frame neural inference at camera frame rates is only realistic on dedicated silicon.
  • Result buffers are fixed-size. Each detection request returns at most 20 rows of 6 floats (app.py L405–407); dense scenes rely on region consolidation and thresholding rather than unlimited outputs.
  • Restart storms are capped. The watchdog gives a process 5 restarts per 60 seconds (watchdog.py L16–17) before backing off — a genuinely flaky accelerator will go quiet instead of thrashing forever.
  • Expect a warm-up. The motion detector calibrates on startup before trusting its own boxes, so detection quality in the first minutes after a restart is not representative.
entry.summary: How Frigate NVR runs local object detection: ffmpeg capture, shared-memory frames, CPU/Coral/OpenVINO/TensorRT detectors, MQTT events and Home Assistant.

entry.title: How Homebridge Works: Inside the HomeKit Bridge Architecture

link.title: How Homebridge Works: Inside the HomeKit Bridge Architecture

entry.content:
You spend a weekend wiring a garage door relay, a cheap Zigbee bulb set, and an off-brand robot vacuum into something controllable — then open the Apple Home app and find none of them. HomeKit is a walled garden by design: it only talks to accessories that speak the HomeKit Accessory Protocol (HAP) and, in practice, carry Apple’s MFi certification. Thousands of excellent devices will never be in that club. Homebridge is the open-source project that quietly ended the argument years ago: a Node.js server that impersonates a genuine HomeKit bridge, so uncertified devices of every kind appear in the Home app as if Apple had blessed them. Pair it with Zigbee2MQTT and the radio side of the house stays open too.

This post dissects how that impersonation works, using two architecture diagrams generated from the homebridge/homebridge repository (default branch latest, version 2.5.0). The overview shows the moving parts; the detail diagram traces the startup chain down to individual functions in src/server.ts, src/pluginManager.ts, src/bridgeService.ts, and src/childBridgeFork.ts, every node linking to real source.

By the end you will know exactly why the boot order is cache → plugins → platforms → publish, why a plugin’s registerAccessory() call only works during initialization, how cached accessory UUIDs survive restarts, what a _bridge config block spawns, and where the new Matter support fits.

Overview: one Server orchestrating plugins, a single HAP Bridge accessory, the accessory cache, and forked child bridges. Every node links to real source in homebridge/homebridge@latest.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process entry point is cli(), L28: it parses flags, points HAPStorage at the persist directory at L73, and only then constructs the Server at L87.
  • Server.start, L208 runs a fixed boot sequence — cache, plugins, platforms, child bridges, and only then the publication that makes it visible to HomeKit.
  • HomebridgeAPI, L635 is one EventEmitter (API version 2.7) handed to every plugin; the registerAccessory overload at L814 converts plugin calls into internal events rather than direct wiring.
  • new Bridge, L334 creates the thing HomeKit actually pairs with: a single hap-nodejs Bridge accessory named from config.json, with the fixed UUID uuid.generate('HomeBridge').
  • publishBridge, L374 builds a PublishInfo (username, port, pincode, Categories.BRIDGE) and calls bridge.publish() at L406.
  • loadCachedPlatformAccessoriesFromDisk, L417 and restoreCachedPlatformAccessories, L483 are the cache halves: read serialized accessories before plugins load, then replay each one into configureAccessory().
  • ChildBridgeService, L216 supervises one forked Node process per _bridge config, created with a real fork() at L424.
  • The protocol itself lives in the @homebridge/hap-nodejs, L53 dependency; this repo is the plugin host and config layer around it.

Detail: the startup chain from cli() through plugin initialization and cache restore to HAP publication, plus the child-bridge fork path. Node labels link to exact lines in the repository.

The Bridge Trick: One HomeKit Accessory for Everything

HAP defines a special accessory type — a bridge — that proxies many bridged accessories over one pairing. Homebridge exploits that to the hilt: you pair once, with the QR code printed by printSetupInfo, L1265, and everything every plugin exposes rides behind that single pairing. The defaults come from loadConfig, L362: bridge name Homebridge, username CC:22:3D:E3:CE:30, PIN 031-45-154 (L366–L370). The username must look like a MAC address — the check at L424 rejects anything else, because hap-nodejs uses it as the pairing identity.

For legacy accessory plugins, each configured instance becomes a hap-nodejs accessory via createHAPAccessory, L768. It calls the plugin’s getServices() at L769, and if the plugin returns an empty set the accessory is silently dropped at L774 — a common source of “my accessory vanished” bug reports. The stable UUID is derived from the accessory type and name at L780, which is why renaming an accessory in config makes HomeKit treat it as a new device.

The Startup Chain: Command to Published Bridge

The detail diagram’s left half is worth internalizing: almost every startup bug is a violation of it. cli() constructs the Server, whose constructor parses the config, creates exactly one HomebridgeAPI, L119 per process, then a PluginManager, L139 and a BridgeService, L151. start() then runs in a fixed order at L208:

  1. Cache first: loadCachedPlatformAccessoriesFromDisk, L216 — so serialized accessories exist in memory before any plugin runs.
  2. Plugins second: initializeInstalledPlugins, L238 imports each plugin and runs its default-exported initializer.
  3. Platforms and accessories third: loadPlatforms, L571 and loadAccessories at L265–L270, with dynamic platforms registered but not yet replayed.
  4. Child bridges start at L273, then cache replay via restoreCachedPlatformAccessories at L278.
  5. api.signalFinished() at L281 emits didFinishLaunching — the event plugins wait for before polling hardware — followed by await Promise.all(promises) at L284 so legacy static platforms finish before publishBridge, L286.

That last ordering is a compatibility contract with the oldest plugin style: a StaticPlatformPlugin hands over accessories through a callback, and loadPlatformAccessories, L817 waits for it while warning every 20 seconds at L821 if a plugin is stalling the whole bridge.

The Plugin API: Three Flavours, One Funnel

Every plugin is an npm package whose default export is a function receiving the api object. initializeInstalledPlugins, L199 iterates discovered plugins, calls plugin.load() (which validates the engines.homebridge requirement and dynamically imports the entry point at L220), then initializePlugin, L235 invokes the initializer with the API instance at L238.

One guard rail worth knowing: handleRegisterAccessory, L255 throws if a plugin registers outside a running initializer — “register later, on a timer” plugins crash.

Homebridge classifies platform plugins by duck-typing, not by declared interface. isDynamicPlatformPlugin, L798 checks whether configureAccessory exists on the instance; isStaticPlatformPlugin, L802 checks for the legacy accessories callback. loadPlatforms, L658 branches on that: dynamic platforms get stored via assignDynamicPlatform, static ones join the awaited promise list, and independent platforms (like config UIs) just get constructed.

Dynamic platforms then manage their own accessories through the API: registerPlatformAccessories, L855 stamps each accessory with _associatedPlugin and _associatedPlatform at L862 before emitting the internal event that BridgeService subscribed to in its constructor at L329. The same pattern handles updates, unregistration, and external accessories — IP cameras and TVs that get their own HAPServer outside the bridge.

The Accessory Cache: Why UUIDs Survive Restarts

HomeKit hates churn: change an accessory’s UUID and the user re-configures rooms, automations, and notifications. Homebridge’s answer is a disk cache at ~/.homebridge/accessories/cachedAccessories, resolved by User.cachedAccessoryPath, L23 over the ~/.homebridge base at L32.

The read path is defensive. loadCachedPlatformAccessoriesFromDisk, L417 reads through the StorageService at L421; on a JSON SyntaxError it falls back to the .cachedAccessories.bak backup named at L452, which is written after every successful load at L441. Each record becomes a PlatformAccessory, L37 — an EventEmitter mirroring a hap-nodejs accessory, with a plugin-writable context field at L55 that survives serialization.

The restore path restoreCachedPlatformAccessories, L483 replays each cached accessory into the matching dynamic platform’s configureAccessory(), and even survives plugin renames: if the recorded _associatedPlugin is missing, L511 searches for a plugin with an active dynamic platform of the same name and rewrites the association. Writes happen at every mutation — L600 for register, L674 for update, L690 for unregister — and once more during teardown at L859, right before the shutdown event reaches plugins.

Child Bridges: One Process Per Plugin

A single misbehaving plugin can block the event loop of the entire bridge, since the process shares one Node.js runtime (see how Node.js works). The escape hatch is the _bridge block in config.json. When loadAccessories, L507 or loadPlatforms, L617 sees _bridge.username, the plugin is routed into a ChildBridgeService, L525 instead of the main bridge, tracked in a map keyed by MAC-style username at L84.

validateChildBridgeConfig, L674 enforces uniqueness: a child username must be valid, must not collide with the main bridge, and each platform child bridge needs its own identity. At runtime the service forks childBridgeFork.js at L424; inside that child, loadPlugin, L88 strips _bridge keys from the config, builds a fresh HomebridgeAPI, L122, and loads exactly one plugin. The child then assembles its own BridgeService at L201 and publishes an independent HomeKit bridge with its own port and pairing code. Restart, stop, and start commands arrive over IPC (L801, L815, L836) — that is how homebridge-config-ui-x restarts one plugin without touching the parent.

From HAP-Only Monolith to Matter-Era Architecture

The build facts tell the story of a decade-long shift. Homebridge began as a monolith containing the entire HAP implementation; today package.json declares version 2.5.0 with @homebridge/hap-nodejs 2.3.0 as a dependency at L53, and the old lib/ HAP sources are gone — under src/types/ only a qrcode-terminal type stub remains. The plugin-facing API has incremented to version 2.7 (L636), and engines now requires Node.js ^22.12.0 || ^24 || ^26 at L33 — the codebase has fully moved to ES modules with dynamic import() for plugin loading.

The bigger leap is Matter. Homebridge 2.x ships an opt-in Matter bridge: Server.start() only dynamically imports MatterBridgeManager, L246 when a bridge.matter block exists, deliberately avoiding the heavy @matter/main stack for HAP-only installs. Plugins get a parallel API surface — the api.matter getter at L689 returns undefined unless Matter is configured, and dynamic platforms can implement configureMatterAccessory at L129 alongside their HAP counterpart. Matter accessories keep their own MatterAccessoryCache, L74, mirroring the HAP cache design. Matter control requests even route to child bridges over IPC, reusing the fork infrastructure built for HAP isolation.

If you want to go further than switching lights, the same pattern composes: Homebridge for HomeKit translation, Node-RED for event-driven automations across both HomeKit and non-HomeKit devices.

Honest Limits

  • No HAP code lives here. Everything protocol-level — pairing, encryption, characteristic I/O, mDNS — is the @homebridge/hap-nodejs dependency. This repo is config validation, plugin lifecycle, and cache management only.
  • Static plugins can stall the boot. A legacy platform that never calls the accessories callback blocks publication; Homebridge only warns every 20 seconds (L821) rather than timing it out.
  • Empty plugin responses vanish silently. An accessory plugin whose getServices() returns nothing is skipped without an error at L774 — by design, but confusing the first time.
  • Orphaned cache entries need -K. Cached accessories whose plugin no longer loads are dropped unless keepOrphanedCachedAccessories is set (cli.ts L50).
  • The default is one shared process. Without _bridge blocks, all plugins run on the main event loop; a blocking plugin delays didFinishLaunching for everything else.
  • Matter is opt-in and partial. Accessory-style child bridges do not support Matter at all — startBridge() warns and ignores the config at L158–L160.

Homebridge’s lesson for anyone building protocol adapters: keep the protocol engine in a dedicated library, expose a narrow event-based API to plugins, and make identity (UUIDs, cache, pairing) explicit and durable. That structure is why thousands of community plugins have outpaced any vendor’s official integration list.
entry.summary: How Homebridge emulates a HomeKit bridge in Node.js: HAP pairing, the plugin API, accessory caching, child bridges and Matter support, traced from the source.
